mcqs.question: Without feature flags, why are 'deploy' and 'release' effectively the same event?
options: Because CI/CD tools technically don't allow separating them
Because rollback is impossible without flags
Because deploying always requires a code review, and reviews imply release
Because the moment new code reaches production, every user is exposed to it — there's no separate gate between shipping the code and users seeing its behavior
mcqs.explanation: With no flag, whatever code runs in production is immediately what every user experiences — there's no independent lever to decide who sees it or when, so the two events collapse into one. Rollback exists via redeploy regardless of flags, and neither review requirements nor tooling limitations are the actual reason.

mcqs.question: A team creates a flag to hide an incomplete feature, but two years later it's still in the codebase, load-bearing for a pricing-tier check. What went wrong?
options: Nothing — permission flags are meant to be permanent
The flag's type drifted — a release flag (meant to be temporary) was repurposed as a permission flag (meant to be permanent) without anyone renaming or reclassifying its intent
The flag service itself has a two-year expiry limit that was missed
Release flags should never be used for incomplete features
mcqs.explanation: The four flag types carry different expected lifetimes, and the failure mode here is a release flag quietly becoming a permanent permission flag without anyone naming that shift — which is exactly why naming a flag's type and expected lifetime at creation matters, so drift like this is visible instead of silent. There's no such expiry mechanism, and release flags are the correct tool for hiding incomplete work.

mcqs.question: A new payment provider integration is misbehaving at 2am. Why does a kill switch resolve this faster than a code rollback?
options: A code rollback isn't possible once a deploy has reached production
Kill switches automatically detect and fix the root cause
A kill switch only works for database-related failures

It's a config flip taking effect in seconds and disabling only the failing path, versus reverting a commit, rebuilding, and redeploying the whole artifact — which also undoes everything else in that deploy
mcqs.explanation: A kill switch is purpose-built for exactly this moment: seconds to flip, and it disables only the specific risky path rather than the entire deploy. A code rollback is still possible at 2am, it's just slower and coarser-grained — it reverts the whole artifact, not just the broken piece. Kill switches disable a path; they don't fix anything automatically, and they apply well beyond database issues.

mcqs.question: In a flag check wrapped in a try/except, why should the exception handler fall through to the legacy/safe path rather than defaulting the flag to 'on'?
options: Defaulting to 'on' when the flag service is unreachable would turn your safety mechanism into a single point of failure — a flag-service outage would silently enable every unproven code path at once
It has no real effect either way since flag services never go down
Defaulting to 'on' is actually the industry-standard safe default
Exceptions should always propagate and crash the request instead
mcqs.explanation: The whole point of a flag is to gate risky code behind an explicit decision — if unreachability defaults to 'on,' an outage in the flag service itself becomes an uncontrolled full rollout of everything it guards, at the worst possible moment. Flag services do fail, crashing the request is worse than a graceful fallback, and 'on' is the opposite of a safe default.

mcqs.question: What's the actual risk of a release flag that's been fully rolled out to 100% but never removed from the code?
options: It slows down the flag evaluation service measurably
Every future change now has to reason about a live conditional whose flag-off path may have rotted, and someone may later flip it assuming it still safely does something
It has no real risk since the flag is at 100% and effectively inert
It automatically reverts to 0% after a fixed period, causing unexpected regressions
mcqs.explanation: A flag stuck at 100% is not inert — the branch and the flag-off code path are still there, untested and drifting from reality, and anyone who later flips it (routine cleanup, a misread dashboard) can trigger a code path nobody has verified in months. Flags don't auto-revert, and the cost is code-health risk, not measurable evaluation latency.
